title: The distance along a round sphere is its central angle
source_anchor: units[0], complete statement, definitions and six proof regions in runs/20261116-sphere-distance/source-only.json
target_statement: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space with \(\dim E=n+1\), where \(n\ge1\), and let \(S=\{z\in E:\|z\|=1\}\). For the literal inclusion \(\iota:S\to E\), give a tangent vector \(v\) at \(z\) the length \(\|D\iota_z(v)\|_E\). Define \(d_S(x,y)\) as the infimum of the lengths of all \(C^1\) paths on the closed unit interval from \(x\) to \(y\), using this induced speed. For every \(x,y\in S\), including coincident and antipodal endpoints, this distance is the angle \(\arccos\langle x,y\rangle\).

source_detail_audit.fidelity_boundary: This identifies the induced length distance of a positive-dimensional unit sphere. It leaves the ambient chord metric unchanged; for antipodal points these two distances are \(2\) and \(\pi\). The condition \(n>0\) is essential for arbitrary endpoint pairs: the two-point sphere has no continuous internal path between its two distinct points. It supplies no global Riemannian bundle instance, general manifold geodesic-existence theorem, transport estimate, stochastic result, or textbook chapter completion. Spherical transport is a possible consumer of the distance identity.
